turns.text: Explain our workforce position in plain terms — pretend I'm a brand-new dean.

Here's the lay of the land for your Advanced Manufacturing programs. San Mateo County CCD is a three-college district in the Bay Area, and this is what the market around it looks like.

Employers across the Bay Area are hiring for roughly 8,150 advanced-manufacturing openings a year. All 26 community colleges in the region together produce about 3,923 program completions a year for that kind of work — which leaves about 4,227 openings a year the region's colleges aren't currently putting graduates into.

Your district's part of that regional output is about 200 completions a year — roughly 5% of the region's total — coming out of 2 programs here: Electronics and Electric Technology (about 9.7 completions a year, against roughly 1,170 openings across the jobs it prepares people for) and Energy Systems Technology (about 11 a year, against roughly 1,000 openings). The sector overall touches 49 different occupations.

One thing to keep straight: the demand figure is region-wide and your supply is your district's slice of the region, so that ~4,227 gap is a Bay Area gap, not yours alone to close. And the supply figures are 3-year averages, so a single recent year can run a bit above or below.

Simplest version: Bay Area employers want about 8,150 advanced-manufacturing workers every year. All the region's colleges together train roughly 3,900 of them — so a lot of those jobs go unfilled by local graduates. Your district trains about 200 a year, through 2 programs. You're a small piece of a big regional shortage.
In one sentence: Bay Area employers need about 8,150 advanced-manufacturing workers a year, the region's colleges train roughly 3,900, and your district produces about 200 of them.
